title: Virgo Cluster Galaxy NGC 4458
caption: Virgo cluster galaxy NGC 4458, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA, and E. Peng (Peking University, Beijing)

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: NGC 4458, listed as VCC 1146, is one of the galaxies Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys photographed for a census of globular star clusters across 100 members of the Virgo cluster. Virgo, about 54 million light-years away, is the nearest large galaxy cluster to Earth.

Globular clusters are tightly packed swarms of old stars, and studying them helps astronomers understand the early, intense bursts of star formation that built galaxies. Hubble's sharp view let the team identify about 90 percent of the globulars in all its observed fields, which mattered most for small galaxies that have only a handful.

The giant elliptical galaxy M87, at the centre of Virgo, has long been known to host more globular clusters than predicted. Galaxies within 130,000 light-years of it had few or none, which suggests M87 stripped them of their clusters. In M87, globulars poor in heavy elements such as iron outnumber metal-rich ones three to one, and many of the metal-poor ones may have come from dwarf galaxies.

understand.summary: Taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. F475W (SDSS g) is shown in blue and F850LP (long pass z) in orange.
understand.eye: The colours are assigned to two separate filter images, one reaching into the near-infrared, so they are not the colours an eye would see.

explore: Lead author Eric Peng of Peking University suggests that star formation near Virgo's core was fast and efficient, perhaps driven by dark matter collapsing sooner there, so many globulars near the centre probably formed early in the cluster's history. Farther out, weaker star formation may have produced only less massive clusters that broke apart over time.
